newsitem.title: USA: US bankers sue Farm Credit Administration on rules.
newsitem.headline: US bankers sue Farm Credit Administration on rules.

text.p: Two major U.S. banking groups said Wednesday they had filed suit against the Farm Credit Administration over new rules expanding the customer base of the federally chartered Farm Credit System.

The lawsuit says the rules overstep FCA's power and asks for a permanent injunction against them, the American Bankers Association and the Independent Bankers Association of America said in a statement.
FCA is the regulator of the Farm Credit System. Banks provide about 40 percent of lending for the U.S. farm sector and FCS members 25 percent.

According to the bank groups, the new FCA rules unlawfully expand FCS lending to businesses that furnish farm-related services to farmers and ranchers, to cooperatives that furnish farm or aquatic business services, to processing and marketing operations, new rural housing authorities and to organizations that are not ag producers.

"By expanding the groups or persons and businesses eligible for FCS credit...the rule now permits FCS lending institutions to offer a broad range of financial services directly competing with those offered by community banks, rather than the special purpose, limited range of services intended by Congress," the bank groups said.

Marsha Martin, who chairs the FCA, has said the new rule "responds to the needs of a changing agriculture." It also gives FCS institutions nationwide "greater flexibility to respond to the credit needs of eligible borrowers," she said one month ago.
ABA and IBAA warned March 11 that they would sue as soon as the new rules took effect. FCA unveiled them in January but they could not go into force until the end of a review period before Congress.
